question: Al, Bert, and Carl are the winners of a school drawing for a pile of Halloween candy, which they are to divide in a ratio of \(3 : 2 : 1,\) respectively. Due to some confusion they come at different times to claim their prizes, and each assumes he is the first to arrive. If each takes what he believes to be his correct share of candy, what fraction of the candy goes unclaimed?
solution:
Each boy believes the pile he finds is the entire prize, so his share is a fraction of the candy present when he arrives. The ratio has \(3+2+1=6\) equal parts. Al therefore takes \(3/6=1/2\) of his pile, Bert takes \(2/6=1/3\), and Carl takes \(1/6\).

It is easier to track what each boy leaves. Al leaves \(1/2\) of the pile he finds, Bert leaves \(2/3\), and Carl leaves \(5/6\). Each visit multiplies the current amount by its remaining fraction, so the fraction of the original candy left after all three visits is
\[
\frac12\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac56
=\boxed{\frac{5}{18}}.
\]
Changing the arrival order only changes the order of these factors, so the result is the same in every case. The answer is choice D.

nodes.description: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number , e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem. For example, if each person at a party will eat 3/8 of a pound of roast beef, and there will be 5 people at the party, how many pounds of roast beef will be needed? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?
nodes.label: 4.NF.B.4c

nodes.description: Interpret the product (a/b) × q as a parts of a partition of q into b equal parts; equivalently, as the result of a sequence of operations a × q ÷ b. For example, use a visual fraction model to show (2/3) × 4 = 8/3, and create a story context for this equation. Do the same with (2/3) × (4/5) = 8/15. (In general, (a/b) × (c/d) = ac/bd.)
nodes.label: 5.NF.B.4a

nodes.description: Solve real world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem.
nodes.label: 5.NF.B.6

nodes.description: Interpret whole-number quotients of whole numbers , e.g., interpret 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share when 56 objects are partitioned equally into 8 shares, or as a number of shares when 56 objects are partitioned into equal shares of 8 objects each. For example, describe a context in which a number of shares or a number of groups can be expressed as 56 ÷ 8.
nodes.label: 3.OA.A.2

nodes.description: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison, e.g., interpret 35 = 5 × 7 as a statement that 35 is 5 times as many as 7 and 7 times as many as 5. Represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as multiplication equations.
nodes.label: 4.OA.A.1

edges.reason: Larger products motivate shortcuts and supply verification examples. Arrays and table products establish swapping/regrouping independently of a two-digit column method.
edges.scope: verifying multiplication laws on multidigit factors

edges.reason: The integer-multiplier case supplies a useful stepping stone and repeated-addition interpretation. The product-of-numerators/product-of-denominators rule follows directly from a part-of-a-part area model without executing the earlier decimal-free integer-multiplier procedure; Gemini confuses this customary progression with necessity.

The endpoint provides explicit quantity-modeling experience that can help translate a fraction-of-a-whole story into an expression. Price and speed formulas do not define a fractional part, so the benefit is preparation only. This final scoped judgment does not treat a prior native acceptance of Claude's rejection as an accepted dependency.
edges.scope: Prior experience representing total, part and multiplicative relationships in application problems

edges.reason: Taking a fraction of a fractional quantity contains a fraction-by-fraction product in the full application repertoire.

Fraction division prepares ratio values with fractional terms. The target expressly permits a simple ratio, and a whole-number pair such as 6 to 3 needs only ordinary division; no fraction-by-fraction division is universal.

The fraction-of-total allocation route computes total times each share fraction. Dividing the total by the sum of ratio terms is an alternative, so the fraction application is a route component rather than a universal dependency.
edges.scope: computing each part as a fraction of the total

edges.reason: Simplifying a ratio can reduce arithmetic. Sharing 60 in the ratio 4 to 6 by ten equal units already gives 24 and 36, so the greatest-common-factor simplification procedure is optional preparation.

Both the unit-part and fraction-of-total methods read the given ratio as relative shares. Simplifying to lowest terms is optional, whereas this meaning is common to the methods. Root checked both endpoint-based reviews; each identifies the stated content or conditional method rather than a curriculum-order claim.
edges.scope: Understanding the ratio terms as relative part counts before allocating a total
